title: The reviewer who never answers
situation: A senior engineer has held my design doc for three weeks. Every reminder got a thumbs-up and nothing else.
tactic: I stopped sending reminders. I booked a 15-minute call through their calendar, not the thread, and put one question in the invite: approve the caching approach, or name the alternative you want. The question was the whole agenda.
outcome: Worked. They gave a yes in the call and two concrete edits, and the doc moved that week. Next time I would ask for a decision date in the first message.

title: Owned the miss before the review
situation: I missed a quarterly target that I owned. My manager was calm, and I was tempted to skip the review and hope nobody asked.
tactic: I opened the review with the miss, its cause and the fix, before she could raise it. Then I asked for a bigger scope, not a raise, and let her name the number when the scope was delivered.
outcome: Partly worked. She trusted the plan more than before. The raise came six months later, after the new scope shipped.

title: The supplier's surprise rush fee
situation: A supplier added a 20 percent rush fee to an order we had already placed, citing market conditions.
tactic: I did not argue about the fee. I replied with the clause from our original quote and offered them two options: keep the agreed price, or cancel and rebook for next month's slot. I gave them one working day to choose.
outcome: Worked. They dropped the fee within a day. Having the signed quote ready made the difference.

title: Dinner that became a debate
situation: Every family dinner with my father-in-law turned into an argument about how we raise our children.
tactic: I stopped answering the argument itself. Each visit I chose one honest question to ask him, and when the topic turned to the children I moved us onto the garden, which we both knew well. I did not try to win the point.
outcome: Mixed. Fewer fights, and he started asking about the garden first. He still raises the children topic now and then. I just do not take the bait.

title: No email before the first hour
situation: I checked email before my first coffee and carried the anxiety of whatever I read through the whole morning.
tactic: I moved the phone out of the bedroom and set one fixed routine for the first hour. When the urge came, I named it and returned to the routine. I kept my attention on the task in front of me, not on the inbox.
outcome: Worked after about three weeks. It is still hard on days with bad news, but the morning rhythm holds.

title: The friend who keeps cancelling
situation: A close friend has cancelled our weekly run four times this month. I felt resentful and was close to stopping the invitations.
tactic: Instead of a sarcastic message, I said what I had noticed and offered two specific times that suited us both. I left the next move with them and did not list the cancellations in the message.
outcome: Worked. We ran that week, and the cancellations stopped for a while. A plain, honest message mattered more than the schedule.
